p: The KJV adds "the Lord." The oldest copies do not have it.

readings.w: NA28, SBL, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort; Codex Alexandrinus (02, 400s), Vaticanus (03, 300s), Ψ (044, 700s or 800s), 048, 0232, 81, 1739; the Latin, the Sahidic Coptic
Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV); Sinaiticus as corrected, K, L, P (025, 800s), 049, 33, 614, most later manuscripts; the Syriac

why: The shorter reading has the oldest witnesses, and "the Lord Jesus Christ" is the familiar form of Paul's greetings, which a copyist would add without thinking. Plummer notes that John's letters never call Jesus "Lord."
b: The first hand of Sinaiticus reads "the Lord" without the second "from"; a few copies leave the whole phrase out.

p: The KJV says "Grace be with you." Most copies read "with us"; a few have "with you" or leave the words out.

readings.w: NA28, SBL, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Byzantine text; Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, P, Ψ, 0232, 33, 1739, part of the later manuscripts; the Sahidic Coptic
Minuscules 5, 81, 945, part of the later manuscripts; an Old Latin copy, some Vulgate copies (KJV "Grace be with you")
Alexandrinus, 630, 1505 and a few others; the Harklean Syriac
readings.en: (grace, mercy and peace, without "there will be with us")

why: "With us" has the widest and oldest support, and it fits the Elder's habit of counting himself in with his readers (1:2). "With you" turns the promise into the usual letter wish.
b: The word list shows no printed Greek edition with "with you" here, so the KJV's "you" agrees with the minority reading.

p: The KJV says the deceivers "are entered into the world." The oldest copies say they "went out."

readings.w: NA28, SBL, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort; Papyrus 74 (600s), Sinaiticus (01, 300s), Alexandrinus (02), Vaticanus (03), Ψ, 33, 81, 1739; the Latin, the Syriac, the Sahidic Coptic; Irenaeus in Latin
Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV "are entered"); P (025), 049, most later manuscripts; the Bohairic Coptic

why: "Went out" has the early and widespread witnesses, and it matches 1 John 4:1, where false prophets have gone out (exelēlythasin) into the world, and 1 John 2:19, where the opponents "went out from us." The two Greek words differ by one prefix.
b: "Went out" may mean that the deceivers left the church (1 John 2:19) or simply that they set out traveling.

a: Then you will not lose what we worked for, but will receive a full reward.
p: Three Greek forms of this sentence: "you... we... you," all "you," or all "we" (KJV).

readings.w: NA28, SBL, Westcott-Hort (the word list). The witness lists are given word by word, and none of them shows one manuscript with this exact combination: "you lose" and "you receive" are in Sinaiticus as corrected, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Ψ, 81, 1739 and many others, while "we worked" is in Vaticanus (first hand spelled ērgasametha, corrected to eirgasametha) and minuscule 181

readings.en: so that you do not lose what we worked for, but receive a full reward
readings.plain: Then you will not lose what we worked for, but will receive a full reward.

readings.w: Tregelles and Tyndale House (the word list shows they lack "we worked"); Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Ψ, 33, 81, 1739 and many others; the Latin, the Syriac, the Bohairic Coptic; Irenaeus in Latin
readings.orig: ἵνα μὴ ἀπολέσητε ἃ εἰργάσασθε, ἀλλὰ μισθὸν πλήρη ἀπολάβητε
readings.en: so that you do not lose what you worked for, but receive a full reward
readings.plain: Then you will not lose what you worked for, but will receive a full reward.

readings.w: Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV "that we lose not those things which we have wrought, but that we receive a full reward"); K, L, P, 049, most later manuscripts; Hilary
readings.orig: ἵνα μὴ ἀπολέσωμεν ἃ εἰργασάμεθα, ἀλλὰ μισθὸν πλήρη ἀπολάβωμεν
readings.en: so that we do not lose what we worked for, but receive a full reward
readings.plain: Then we will not lose what we worked for, but will receive a full reward.

why: The Plain English Translation follows NA28, whose text in the Catholic Letters is the Editio Critica Maior's. The mixed reading ("you... we... you") is the hardest, and the other two look like copyists making all three verbs match. Plummer judged it the original for that reason. The word list shows that Tyndale House and Tregelles do not have "we worked"; "you worked" has early and wide support, and the two are close. NA28 and the SBL text agree here.
b: With "we worked," the Elder and the first teachers did the work and the readers will reap it. With "you worked," the readers risk losing their own labor.

p: The KJV says "whosoever transgresseth." The oldest copies say "whoever goes ahead."

readings.w: NA28, SBL, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort; Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02), Vaticanus (03), 048, 0232; some Vulgate copies, the Coptic
Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV); P, Ψ, 33, 81, 1739, most later manuscripts; an Old Latin copy, some Vulgate copies, the Syriac; Lucifer of Cagliari

why: "Goes ahead" is the older and the harder reading. It is a strange thing to blame someone for, so a copyist would replace it with the familiar "transgresses"; no one would change "transgresses" into "goes ahead."
b: Plummer offered two meanings for "goes ahead": one who sets himself up as a leader, or one who "goes on beyond the Gospel" into a supposedly higher teaching. He preferred the second: the deceivers counted themselves advanced thinkers. Advancing in that sense means not remaining.

p: The KJV repeats "of Christ" in the second half of the verse. The oldest copies do not.

p: Some Latin copies add: "See, I have told you beforehand, so that you may not be put to shame on the day of our Lord."

why: The sentence is in no Greek copy. It is a Latin addition that rounds off the rule with a warning about the judgment.

p: One Greek letter apart. NA28 and the KJV read "our"; the SBL text and Westcott-Hort read "your."

readings.w: NA28, Tyndale House, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "that our joy may be full"); Sinaiticus (01), K, L, P, Ψ, 614, 1505, most later manuscripts; the Syriac
SBL, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; Alexandrinus (02), Vaticanus (03), 33, 81, 1739, 1881; an Old Latin copy, the Bohairic Coptic

why: The witnesses are divided, and hēmōn and hymōn sounded alike when read aloud. The Plain English Translation follows NA28, whose text here is the Editio Critica Maior's; "our" also fits the Elder's habit of joining himself to his readers (1:2-3). "Your" matches the wording of John 16:24, which copyists may have had in mind.
b: The same choice comes up at 1 John 1:4. Plummer, writing long before the Editio Critica Maior, preferred "your" with Alexandrinus and Vaticanus.

p: The KJV says "I trust to come unto you." Older copies say "to be with you."

why: "To be with you" (genesthai) has the older witnesses and is the less usual verb here; "come" is the easier word a copyist would put in. The meaning hardly changes.

p: The KJV ends with "Amen." Some copies add a blessing, or name the sister church.

why: The oldest copies end without "Amen" or a blessing. Copyists rounded off the letter with the words used when it was read in church.
b: Two other changes touch the sister. Minuscule 307 and some Vulgate copies read "the church" in place of "the chosen one" ("the children of your sister, the church"), and a note in the margin of minuscule 465 reads "the chosen one who is in Ephesus," a later reader placing the sister church in Ephesus.
